prompt: When does ARC free a class instance?

choices.text: When the program is short of memory
choices.why: That describes a collector; ARC frees on a line you can point to, whatever memory is left.

choices.text: On the line where its last strong reference goes
choices.why: Right: the count reaches zero there, and `deinit` runs before the next line.

choices.text: At the end of the function that created it, whatever else holds it
choices.why: Only if no other reference holds it by then; `second` kept the session past `first = nil`.

choices.text: When nothing reachable points at it
choices.why: That is a collector's rule, and section 03 is the case where the two differ.

prompt: In `Arc.swift`, which line printed `session of 45 freed` just after it ran?

choices.text: `first = nil`
choices.why: `second` still held it, so the count went from two to one.

choices.text: `second = nil`
choices.why: Right: the last strong reference let go, and the count reached zero.

choices.text: `var second = first`
choices.why: Assigning a class instance adds a reference; it frees nothing.

choices.text: The last line of the program
choices.why: It was freed in the middle, before `both are nil` was printed.

prompt: Which of these are counted by ARC? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An instance of a `final class`
choices.why: Yes: every class instance carries a count.

choices.text: A `struct` holding two `Int`s
choices.why: No: a struct is a value, copied on assignment.

choices.text: A closure stored in a property
choices.why: Yes: a stored closure is a reference, which is how section 06's cycle forms.

choices.text: An `enum` case
choices.why: No: an enum is a value type.

prompt: `Cycle.swift` printed no `deinit` line at all. Why?

choices.text: `deinit` runs only when the whole program exits, never before
choices.why: `Arc.swift` showed `deinit` running in the middle of the program.

choices.text: `plan()` never returned
choices.why: It printed `plan() is returning` and the program went on.

choices.text: The course and the session hold each other strongly
choices.why: Right: each count stays at one after `plan()` returns, so neither reaches zero.

choices.text: A `final class` has no `deinit` call
choices.why: `final` only forbids subclasses.

prompt: A screen object holds a timer object, and the timer holds the screen to refresh it. Both properties are ordinary. What happens each time the user leaves the screen?

choices.text: The screen is freed, and the timer with it
choices.why: The timer's reference keeps the screen's count above zero.

choices.text: The compiler refuses to build the pair
choices.why: Section 03 compiled a cycle with no warning: each property is fine on its own.

choices.text: Both stay in memory, and the timer keeps firing
choices.why: Right: a cycle, repeated each visit, with live timers inside it.

choices.text: The app crashes on leaving the screen
choices.why: A cycle crashes nothing; it keeps memory, which is why it goes unnoticed.

prompt: A loop of strong references with nothing outside pointing in is a retain ___.
What does a `weak` reference become when the object it pointed to is freed?

choices.text: `nil`
choices.why: Right: Swift sets it, which is why it must be an optional `var`.

choices.text: A copy of the object, kept alive
choices.why: Nothing is copied; the reference simply has nothing to point to.

choices.text: A dangling pointer that crashes when read
choices.why: That is what `unowned` guards against by stopping the program.

choices.text: A strong reference, to keep the object
choices.why: A weak reference never turns strong on its own.

prompt: Why does `weak let course: Course` not compile?
hint: Something has to change it, and to what.

choices.text: `weak` works only on structs
choices.why: It is the opposite: only class references can be weak.

choices.text: Swift must be able to set it to `nil` later
choices.why: Right: so it has to be a `var`, and of an optional type.

choices.text: A `let` cannot hold a class instance
choices.why: `let session = StudySession(...)` holds one in every program here.

choices.text: Properties of a `final class` are read-only
choices.why: `sessions` is a `var` property of a final class.

prompt: A course and its sessions point at each other. Which reference should be `weak`?

choices.text: The course's `sessions` array
choices.why: Then nothing would own the sessions, and they would be freed as soon as they were added.

choices.text: The session's `course` property
choices.why: Right: the parent holds the child strongly, and the child points back weakly.

choices.text: Both, to be safe from every cycle at once
choices.why: With both weak, nothing but local names would hold either object.

choices.text: Neither: ARC finds the loop by itself
choices.why: ARC counts; it does not look for loops.

prompt: In `Weak.swift`, how many strong references hold the course just after `plan()` returns?
hint: The session's reference is weak, and `swift` was local.

prompt: What happens when code reads an `unowned` reference whose object has been freed?

choices.text: It reads `nil`
choices.why: That is `weak`; an unowned reference is not optional.

choices.text: It reads whatever is in that memory now
choices.why: Swift checks, and does not read freed memory quietly.

choices.text: The program stops with a fatal error that says what it read
choices.why: Right: `Attempted to read an unowned reference but object … was already destroyed`.

choices.text: The object is created again
choices.why: Nothing re-creates an object that was freed.

prompt: A teammate writes `unowned let course` in a session, arguing courses always outlive sessions. A year later, sessions are cached for an offline mode. What is the risk?

choices.text: None, as `unowned` adapts to the new owner
choices.why: `unowned` is a promise written once; it does not follow later changes.

choices.text: One read after the parent is freed stops the program
choices.why: Right: the promise was true when written and stopped being true far from that line.

choices.text: A retain cycle between the cache and the course
choices.why: `unowned` adds no strong reference, so it cannot close a loop.

choices.text: A compile error
choices.why: The compiler cannot see lifetimes across a cache.

choices.text: The Kotlin one

prompt: Why can a closure passed to `map` use `self` without risk of a cycle?

choices.text: `map` copies `self` before calling it
choices.why: Nothing is copied; the closure simply does not outlive the call.

choices.text: Closures never capture `self`
choices.why: Section 06's stored closure did, and leaked.

choices.text: It does not escape
choices.why: Right: only a stored closure can be one half of a loop.

choices.text: `map` captures `self` weakly by default
choices.why: There is no such default; the closure is simply short-lived.

prompt: To capture `self` without adding to its count, a stored closure starts with the capture list `[___ self]`.
Put the steps of `weakReport()`'s closure in the order they happen when it runs after the countdown is freed.
What does LeakSanitizer report?

choices.text: Every object that has a `deinit`
choices.why: A `deinit` says nothing about whether an object leaked.

choices.text: Memory nothing reachable points to, at exit
choices.why: Right: a cycle is two blocks reachable only from each other.

choices.text: Every strong reference in the program, with its count
choices.why: It reports leaked memory, and no counts.

choices.text: The lines where `weak` was missing
choices.why: It shows where the leaked memory was allocated, not where a fix goes.

prompt: How many bytes did LeakSanitizer report leaked for `Cycle.swift`?
Why did section 07 pipe the sanitized program through `swift demangle`?

choices.text: To remove the linker's warnings
choices.why: Those came from the build, and `grep -c` counted them.

choices.text: To run the leak check a second time, faster
choices.why: `swift demangle` reads text; it runs nothing.

choices.text: To read the mangled names
choices.why: Right: `$s4main6CourseC4name…` becomes `Course.__allocating_init(name:)`.

choices.text: To restore the `print` lines the sanitizer lost
choices.why: Those were never written; demangling cannot bring them back.

prompt: You suspect a leak in an app's settings screen and you have only a Linux machine with this toolchain. What is the cheapest first check?

choices.text: Open Xcode's memory graph
choices.why: Xcode does not exist on Linux.

choices.text: Rewrite every stored property in the screen's classes as `unowned`
choices.why: That trades a leak for crashes, without finding anything.

choices.text: Make every class a struct and every struct a class
choices.why: A rewrite is not a check.

choices.text: A printing `deinit` in the suspects, then leave the screen
choices.why: Right: a missing `deinit` line names the object to look at.

prompt: Which of these pairs can form a retain cycle?
hint: Something has to be counted on both sides.

choices.text: Two structs, each holding the other in an array
choices.why: Structs are copied, not counted; and a struct cannot contain itself this way.

choices.text: A class and a closure of its own using `self`
choices.why: Right: section 06's leak.

choices.text: A class and an `Int` property
choices.why: An `Int` points at nothing.

choices.text: A class and a `weak` property back to its parent
choices.why: The weak side does not count, which is section 04's fix.

prompt: A `Countdown` stores `onFinish` and the closure uses `self`. Which changes stop the leak? Choose all that apply.
hint: Break one arrow of the loop.

choices.text: `[weak self]` in the closure, with `guard let self`
choices.why: Yes: the closure no longer counts.

choices.text: Set `onFinish = nil` after calling it
choices.why: Yes: the object lets go of the closure, so the loop opens.

choices.text: Mark the class `final`
choices.why: `final` changes inheritance, not references.

choices.text: Write `self.course` instead of `course`
choices.why: That only makes the capture visible; it is still strong.

prompt: Which statement about ARC is true?

choices.text: It frees objects at unpredictable moments
choices.why: ARC is deterministic: the same lines, every run.

choices.text: It needs a `deinit` to free an object
choices.why: `deinit` is optional; it only lets you act on the way out.

choices.text: It finds and breaks retain cycles
choices.why: It cannot see a loop; you break it with `weak` or `unowned`.

choices.text: It counts strong references
choices.why: Right: and frees the instance when the count reaches zero.
